---
title: "Setup"
subtitle: "What to install before the workshop, and how to check it"
---

The workshop is worked in R, inside an IDE, with a ready-made IDE workspace that you download once. An IDE (an integrated development environment, such as Positron, RStudio or VS Code) is the program in which you open files, write and run code and read results. R is the language that does the calculation, and the two are installed separately. The default IDE for the workshop is Positron, because Positron is one of the data-science tools that the workshop teaches, and it is the IDE that the facilitator uses on the shared screen. If you already work in RStudio or in VS Code you can stay there: every task runs in all three, and the module [Positron and other IDEs](tools/ide.qmd) takes you through Positron and says how the tasks are done in the other two.

The IDE workspace and its setup check come from your case study's website, and that site says how to download the workspace and what its folder holds. Steps 1 to 3 below cover the three tools that every workspace needs, and step 4 runs the check.

Windows and Linux installations are supported in class. macOS installations are not, because the facilitator does not use a Mac and cannot test one. The Mac steps below follow the official documentation and link to it, and a Mac user who gets stuck should work from those links or from the [help page](help.qmd), since no in-class assistance is available for a Mac.

---

## 1. R

R is the language in which the analysis is written. Positron requires R 4.2 or later, and the check script of every IDE workspace expects R 4.4 or later. Download R from [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/) and use the installer for your system.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Windows

Download the installer from the [CRAN Windows page](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/) and run it. Accept the defaults, with one exception: keep the box **"Save version number in registry"** ticked, because RStudio, Positron and the VS Code R extension all use the registry entry to find R. Rtools, the toolchain for compiling packages from source, is not needed for the workshop, because every package that the workshop uses installs as a pre-built binary.

### macOS

The [CRAN macOS page](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/) offers two builds of the current release, and you need the one that matches your machine: the **Apple silicon (arm64)** package for an M-series Mac, which requires macOS 14 or later, and the **Intel (x86_64)** package for an Intel Mac, which requires macOS 11 or later. Open the `.pkg` and follow the installer. If macOS refuses the installer access to your Downloads folder, move the file to your home folder and run it from there, as the CRAN page advises. XQuartz is only needed for the X11 graphics device, which the workshop does not use. The [R for macOS FAQ](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/RMacOSX-FAQ.html) is the reference for anything that the installer does not settle, and the [R-SIG-Mac list](https://stat.ethz.ch/mailman/listinfo/r-sig-mac) is where Mac-specific problems are discussed.

### Linux

Install R from the packages of your distribution or from the repositories maintained by CRAN, which are more current: the [Ubuntu](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/), [Debian](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/linux/debian/) and [Fedora and Red Hat](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/linux/fedora/) pages give the repository lines to add. On Linux, packages are usually compiled from source when they are installed, so the build tools and the development headers for `libcurl`, `libssl` and `libxml2` should be present. The CRAN pages for each distribution list the package names.

:::

On macOS and Linux, open a terminal afterwards and type `R --version`: a version line means that R is installed and on your path. On Windows that test misleads, because the installer does not add R to the path and PowerShell reads `R` as a command of its own, which repeats an earlier command, so the reply is an error even when R is installed. Look instead for the R entry with the version that you installed in the Start menu. Positron and RStudio find R through the registry entry, and step 4 checks the whole installation.

---

## 2. Quarto

Quarto is the tool that turns your report, a `.qmd` file holding code and prose, into a finished document, and rendering the report is how your preregistration block gets its date. Whether you need to install it depends on the IDE:

- **RStudio** comes with a copy of Quarto inside it, so nothing more is needed to render; installing Quarto separately from [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) gets you a newer version than the bundled one, which is worth doing but not required.
- **Positron** ships with the Quarto extension, which gives it the render and preview commands. Positron also includes the Quarto command-line tool (Quarto 1.10.18 in Positron 2026.10.2), so its render and preview commands work without a separate installation. In that release the bundled copy is also on the path of the terminals and of the R session that Positron starts, so the check script of the IDE workspace (step 4 below) finds it. If the check reports a FAIL on its Quarto line, which can happen with other releases, install Quarto from [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).
- **VS Code** needs both the Quarto extension and the Quarto command-line tool, which you install from [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).

To confirm a separate installation, open a fresh terminal and type `quarto --version`.

---

## 3. The IDE

Pick one. The default for the workshop is Positron, and the other two are fully supported for every task.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Positron

Positron is a data-science IDE from Posit, built on the same open-source foundation as VS Code and free to use. Download it from [positron.posit.co/download](https://positron.posit.co/download.html).

- **Windows** 10 or later on x64, and Windows 11 on ARM64; the installer comes in a per-user and a system-wide version, and Positron asks for the latest Visual C++ Redistributable, which the installer points you to if it is missing.
- **macOS** 11 or later, with separate downloads for Apple silicon and Intel machines. Open the `.dmg` and drag Positron to Applications.
- **Linux** with `.deb` packages for Ubuntu 20 and later and Debian, and `.rpm` packages for Red Hat 9 and Fedora, on x64 and ARM64.

When Positron first opens it finds the R you installed in step 1 on its own, looking in the standard locations for your system and, on Windows, in the registry entry that the R installer wrote. Its welcome page shows an environment card that checks whether R is ready and offers to fix what it finds. The Quarto extension and R language support are built in, so there is nothing to add. If you are coming from RStudio, open the settings, search for "RStudio keybindings", tick the box and restart Positron, so that the keyboard shortcuts you know carry over.

### RStudio

RStudio is the IDE that most R users learned on, and if it is already on your machine you can use it as it is. Install R first, then download RStudio Desktop from [posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). In September 2026 the current release is 2026.09. It runs on Windows 11, on macOS 14 or later, and on Ubuntu 22 and later, Debian 13, Red Hat 9 and 10 and Fedora, as an `.exe`, a `.dmg` or a `.deb` and `.rpm` package. RStudio finds R on its own and includes a copy of Quarto, so steps 1 and 3 are all it needs. Open the IDE workspace as a project (step 4).

### VS Code

VS Code is the general-purpose editor on which Positron is built, and it works for R once two extensions and one R package are in place. Download it from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/download). Then, inside VS Code, install the **R** extension (`REditorSupport.r`) and the **Quarto** extension (`quarto.quarto`) from the Extensions view. In R, install the package that gives the editor its code completion and diagnostics: `install.packages("pak")` once, if `pak` is not installed yet, then `pak::pak("languageserver")`. On Windows the R extension finds R through the registry entry from step 1, and on any system you can point it at an R executable in the settings of the extension (`r.rpath.windows`, `r.rpath.mac`, `r.rpath.linux`). Two optional extras, the `radian` console and the `httpgd` package for the plot viewer, are described in the [VS Code R documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/languages/r). The Quarto command-line tool is installed separately (step 2).

:::

---

## 4. Check that it works {#check-that-it-works}

Open the unzipped folder of the IDE workspace in your IDE, because every path in the workspace is relative to that folder. In **Positron** and in **VS Code**, choose **File → Open Folder** and pick the folder; the files appear in a panel on the left. In **RStudio**, open the `.Rproj` file inside the folder, and RStudio opens the folder as a project with the working directory set.

In the folder, open `R/check_setup.R` and run it: click **Run** or **Source** in your IDE, or type `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the R console. The script prints an OK or FAIL line for each check: your R version, Quarto, the packages that the IDE workspace uses and each data file. The script changes nothing on your system. If any package is missing, it prints a line of R that installs all the missing packages at once, at the versions with which the workshop was tested, so run that line and then run the script again. Quarto cannot be installed from R in this way. If the script says that Quarto is not found, install it (step 2) and run the script again in a fresh session. Fix any FAIL before the day.

If something fails and the script does not say why, the [help page](help.qmd) lists the problems that other participants have met, with their fixes and with prompts you can give an AI assistant. If the installation still fails, the slides used in a session and the webR workspace of your case study run the same tasks inside the browser.
